newsitem.title: UK: Predators scent blood in Ivory & Sime saga.
newsitem.headline: Predators scent blood in Ivory & Sime saga.

text.p: The resignation of Colin Hook, controversial chief of Edinburgh fund management company Ivory & Sime, has increased its vulnerability to take-over despite assertions that it is not for sale, fund managers said on Tuesday.

Hook quit as managing director of the fund management firm on Monday and left immediately because of alleged difficulties in his relationship with fund managers, four of whom left last month to set up their own firm.
Industry sources say persistent management troubles at the blue chip firm, listed on the London Stock Exchange, have made it a target for predators seeking an investment management arm.
"People scent blood on the water," said one industry analyst who declined to be named. "I'm sure there will be people having discussions with Caledonia on whether they wish to part with their stake."
Caledonia Investments is the Cayzer family company which owns nearly 30 percent of Ivory & Sime.
A London fund manager said the Scottish firm has "inexplicably, and repeatedly, pressed the self-destruct button" in the last few years.
"Most of the brokers regard them in play," added a top Edinburgh-based fund manager. "Their investment trusts give stability to their income and that makes them attractive."
David Kinloch, who moves from non-executive to executive chairman to replace Hook, said on Monday the firm was not looking for offers and its business was in good shape despite the defections.

With about 4.0 billion pounds under management, Ivory & Sime is not a major player in international terms. It has little pension fund expertise and has not grown funds under management over the past 10 years, unlike bigger rivals which have expanded by a factor of five.
But the stability of its investment trusts, its Charlotte Square address and history -- it recently celebrated its centenary -- would make it a desirable acquisition.
The industry analyst said the house could prove attractive to a foreign firm such as Old Mutual, ABN AMRO or Dresdner Bank, all of which have stated their desire to move into asset management
"The main plank of Ivory & Sime is their investment trust business, so it would only be a stepping stone (for a potential predator)," he said.

"If a major European bank came in to buy Ivory & Sime it would not be the only deal it would want to do...Such a move would not satisfy their ambitions since they would want more growth in assets under management."

The Edinburgh-based fund manager said the boards of the investment trusts under Ivory & Sime management would have to give a guarantee that the management contract would stay with Ivory & Sime, as occurred when Edinburgh Fund Managers took over the Dunedin fund group a year ago.

But the industry analyst said changes were unlikely soon. "Short-term nothing will happen. I think they will try to nurse it back to health and performance has been better over the last few months, so that should be encouraging for clients," he said.
"They've got some breathing space, but not a huge amount. They will have to sort out the people thing in the first half of 1997."
